title: Against slavery
hook: slow at first, Emerson came to speak strongly against slavery

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Margaret Fuller, who asked that every path be opened to women. Your line was equal minds.

An honest thing to say about a man this path has spent weeks with: on the great moral wound of his country, Emerson was slow. He believed slavery was wrong, and said so in his journals. But for a long stretch he kept mostly to his study and his lectures, wary of crowds and causes and movements. Others moved sooner. By the usual account, his own wife was involved in antislavery work in Concord before he was. And people who had escaped slavery were already speaking out, at a risk he never faced. Then something changed, and the quiet man in the study stood up.
screen: `HE BELIEVED IT WAS WRONG.` → `HE STAYED IN THE STUDY.` → `THEN HE STOOD UP.`

segments.voice: First, his reasons for waiting. Emerson distrusted joining things. Self-reliance, for him, meant reforming your own soul before reforming the world, and he worried causes could swallow a person whole. There's something real in that worry. There's also something convenient in it, and later readers have said so plainly. Second, what changed. His country passed the Fugitive Slave Law, which required people in free states to help return those who had escaped slavery. Now the wrong wasn't happening somewhere else. It reached into Concord and asked him to cooperate. In his journal he wrote, in effect, that he would not obey it. Third, what he did. He began speaking in public, and sharply. He turned against Daniel Webster, a statesman he had long admired, for supporting the law. He spoke for the cause, and he welcomed the abolitionist John Brown to Concord. Whatever one thinks of every choice he made, the careful man had stopped being careful. Fourth, what it shows. A good person can hold the right belief for years and still keep it indoors. Agreeing silently felt like enough, until something made it impossible. Speaking up isn't being loud about everything. It's the moment a private conviction walks out of the study, into a room where it might cost you something.
screen: `REFORM THE SOUL FIRST.` · `THE LAW REACHED INTO CONCORD.` · `HE TURNED ON A MAN HE ADMIRED.` · `THE CONVICTION LEAVES THE STUDY.` · then, large: `SPEAK UP.`

segments.voice: Let your mind go to one wrong near you, at work, at school, in the family: not the biggest in the world, the nearest. Notice the reasons you've given for staying quiet, some wise, some just comfortable, without sorting them yet. Then picture one plain sentence you could say about it to one person, and hold it.
Against slavery. Emerson believed slavery was wrong for years before he spoke strongly; a law that asked for his cooperation brought him out of his study. Today's word.
Your line: speak up. A conviction kept indoors can wait too long. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often study his later antislavery speeches alongside his early caution, as a case of a private conviction becoming public action.

chat.says: Emerson was against slavery, right? So why do people call him slow?
options: He believed it was wrong for years but kept quiet, until the Fugitive Slave Law pulled him out.
He spoke out from the very start, but people at the time mostly ignored what he said.
He never spoke publicly about it at all; he only wrote about it in his private journals.
chat.meaning: Emerson held the right belief for years but kept to his study. The Fugitive Slave Law asked for his cooperation, and he began speaking out sharply.

Journal paraphrase: Emerson's 1851 journal is commonly quoted as 'I will not obey it, by God.' The script paraphrases. Confirm.
'By the usual account, his own wife was involved in antislavery work in Concord before he was': Lidian Emerson and the Concord Female Anti-Slavery Society. Confirm wording.

John Brown's visits to Concord and Emerson's support are mentioned briefly, with 'whatever one thinks of every choice he made'. A reviewer should check this is handled carefully, given Brown's violence.
